facts.fact_text: On 6 May 2012 a public demonstration entitled the 'March of Millions' was held in central Moscow.
The march on 6 May 2012 was peaceful and held without any disruptions.
According to the applicant, on 6 May 2012 he arrived at Kaluzhskaya Square to take part in the 'March of Millions' demonstration.
To control the crowd at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012, the police cordon forced the protestors to remain within the barriers.
There were numerous clashes between the police and protestors at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
At 5.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the police ordered the meeting at Bolotnaya Square to finish early.
At 5.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the police began to disperse the participants of the meeting at Bolotnaya Square.
The applicant was arrested by the police on 6 May 2012 and taken to a police station before being released shortly after.
On 26 July 2012 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of having participated in acts of mass disorder on 6 May 2012.

On 6 May 2012 the Moscow city department of the Investigative Committee of the Russian Federation opened criminal proceedings to investigate suspected acts of mass disorder under Article 212 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.

On 6 May 2012 the Moscow city department of the Investigative Committee of the Russian Federation opened criminal proceedings to investigate suspected violence against the police under Article 318 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.
On 18 May 2012 the criminal file opened on 6 May 2012 was transferred to the headquarters of the Investigative Committee of the Russian Federation for further investigation.
On 28 May 2012 an investigation was launched into the criminal offence of organising acts of mass disorder under Article 212 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.
On 28 May 2012 the two criminal cases (mass disorder and organising mass disorder) were joined into a single case.
At the time of his arrest the applicant was a second-year student at the Moscow University of Social Studies.
At the time of his arrest the applicant worked part-time as a courier for an insurance company.
The Basmannyy District Court's detention order of 27 July 2012 referred to the gravity of the charges against the applicant.

The Basmannyy District Court's detention order of 27 July 2012 referred to information about the applicant's character, including a report by Moscow Police's chief of department at the Centre for Counter-Extremism.
According to the report by Moscow Police's chief of department at the Centre for Counter-Extremism, the applicant was an active member of organisations of a destructive character.

According to the report by Moscow Police's chief of department at the Centre for Counter-Extremism, if the applicant were to stay at liberty, he planned to threaten witnesses, abscond and obstruct the investigation.
The Basmannyy District Court concluded on 27 July 2012 that the circumstances gave sufficient grounds to believe that the applicant was likely to flee to avoid the investigation and trial.

The Basmannyy District Court concluded on 27 July 2012 that the circumstances gave sufficient grounds to believe that the applicant was likely to destroy evidence or otherwise obstruct the investigation of the criminal case, which was still at an initial stage.
On 1 August 2012 charges were brought against the applicant under Article 212 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation (participation in acts of mass disorder accompanied by violence).
The applicant was accused of resisting police officers by pushing them away when they were arresting other protestors.
The applicant was accused of trying to liberate protestors who were being arrested by police officers.
On 27 August 2012 the Moscow City Court upheld the detention order of 27 July 2012 issued by the Basmannyy District Court.
On 24 September 2012 the Basmannyy District Court examined an application from the investigator for an extension of the applicant's pre-trial detention.
At the hearing on 24 September 2012 the applicant asked for the preventive measure to be changed to house arrest.
At the hearing on 24 September 2012 the applicant asked for the preventive measure to be changed to a written undertaking not to leave a specified place.
At the hearing on 24 September 2012 the applicant asked for the preventive measure to be changed to bail.
At the hearing on 24 September 2012 the applicant asked for the preventive measure to be changed to personal guarantees.
On 24 September 2012 the Basmannyy District Court granted the investigator's application and extended the applicant's pre-trial detention until 6 November 2012.
The Basmannyy District Court's extension order of 24 September 2012 was based on the finding that the circumstances justifying the original detention order had not changed.
On 1 October 2012 Police Officer T. identified the applicant during an identification parade as a participant in mass disorder who had used violence against him.
Police Officer T. stated that when he and other officers had been arresting a protester, the applicant had grabbed T.'s hand and pulled it off the protestor, thereby causing Police Officer T. pain.
Police Officer L. identified the applicant during an identification parade as a participant in acts of mass disorder who had tried to prevent the police from arresting another protestor.
On 22 October 2012 the Moscow City Court dismissed the applicant's appeal against the extension order of 24 September 2012 issued by the Basmannyy District Court.
On 29 October 2012 the Basmannyy District Court granted an extension of the applicant's pre-trial detention until 6 March 2013, essentially on the same grounds as earlier.
The Basmannyy District Court's extension order of 29 October 2012 noted that the circumstances justifying the detention order had not changed.
In the extension order of 29 October 2012 the Basmannyy District Court dismissed an objection from the applicant to the use of the operational-search reports concerning his character.
In the extension order of 29 October 2012 the Basmannyy District Court rejected the applicant's contesting of the alleged membership of any organisations of a destructive nature.
On 15 November 2012 the charges against the applicant were reformulated.
On 21 December 2012 the charges against the applicant were reformulated.
The reformulated charges stated that the applicant had been wearing a surgical mask to conceal his face during the events of 6 May 2012.
The reformulated charges stated that the applicant had used violence against the police while trying to liberate protestors who had been arrested.
The reformulated charges stated that the applicant had pushed police officers away.
The reformulated charges stated that the applicant had grabbed Police Officer T.'s hand and pulled it off a protester, thereby preventing his arrest.
The reformulated charges stated that the applicant had built a line of metal barriers to block the police and had tried to repel the police with them.
The applicant's alleged offences were additionally classified under Article 318 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation (use of violence against a public official).
On 5 March 2013 the Basmannyy District Court granted a new extension of the applicant's pre-trial detention until 6 July 2013, essentially on the same grounds as before.
On 17 April 2013 the Moscow City Court upheld the extension order of 5 March 2013 issued by the Basmannyy District Court.
On 24 May 2013 the applicant's criminal case was transferred to the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow for the determination of criminal charges.
On 6 June 2013 the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow granted another extension of the applicant's pre-trial detention until 24 November 2013.
The extension order of 6 June 2013 by the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow concerned eleven defendants.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court's extension order of 6 June 2013 was based on the gravity of the charges and the finding that 'the reasons which initially warranted the detention have not changed'.
The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court's extension order of 6 June 2013 was based on the finding that 'no other measures of restraint would secure the aims and goals of the judicial proceedings'.

The applicant's request for an alternative preventive measure was dismissed by the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court on 6 June 2013 on the grounds that no other measure could secure the proper course of justice in the case.
On 2 July 2013 the Moscow City Court upheld the extension order of 6 June 2013 issued by the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow.
On 19 November 2013 the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow granted another extension of pre-trial detention in respect of nine defendants, including the applicant, until 24 February 2014.
The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court's extension order of 19 November 2013 was based on the gravity of the charges and the nature of the offences imputable to the defendants.
On 17 December 2013 the Moscow City Court upheld the extension order of 19 November 2013 issued by the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow.
The applicant was held in remand prison IZ-77/2 for the whole period of his pre-trial detention from 4 September 2012.
According to the applicant, the conditions of his detention in remand prison IZ-77/2 had been poor.

The applicant referred to Lind v. Russia (no. 25664/05, §§ 42 and 58-63, 6 December 2007), in which the Court had previously found a breach of Article 3 of the Convention because of overcrowding in remand prison IZ-77/2 in 2004-2005.

The applicant referred to Zentsov and Others v. Russia (no. 35297/05, §§ 25-29 and 40-44, 23 October 2012), in which the Court had previously found a breach of Article 3 of the Convention because of overcrowding in remand prison IZ-77/2 in 2004-2005.

The applicant referred to Vyatkin v. Russia (no. 18813/06, §§ 26-27 and 38-43, 11 April 2013), in which the Court had previously found a breach of Article 3 of the Convention because of overcrowding in remand prison IZ-77/2 in 2004-2005.

The applicant submitted that his conditions of detention in remand prison IZ-77/2 had been similar to those found to breach Article 3 of the Convention in the cases of Lind v. Russia, Zentsov and Others v. Russia, and Vyatkin v. Russia.

The applicant's description of the conditions of detention during transfer from the remand prison to court and back was identical to those described in Yaroslav Belousov v. Russia (nos. 2653/13 and 60980/14, §§ 69-73, 4 October 2016).

The Government's submissions regarding the conditions of detention during transfer from the remand prison to court and back were identical to those in Yaroslav Belousov v. Russia (nos. 2653/13 and 60980/14, §§ 69-73, 4 October 2016).
The applicant submitted that the convoy room of the Moscow City Court was poorly lit.
The applicant submitted that access to the toilet in the convoy room of the Moscow City Court was limited to once an hour.
The applicant submitted that he had been required to strip naked and to perform sit-ups during the body search conducted in the convoy room of the Moscow City Court.
On 6 June 2013 court proceedings began in hearing room no. 338 at the Moscow City Court.
At the end of July 2013 the court proceedings moved from hearing room no. 338 to hearing room no. 635 at the Moscow City Court.
The defendants, including the applicant, were held in glass cabins in hearing room no. 338 and hearing room no. 635 at the Moscow City Court.
From mid-September 2013 to the end of 2013 the hearings continued at the Nikulinskiy District Court of Moscow in hearing room no. 303.
In January and February 2014 the hearings took place at the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow in hearing room no. 410.

Hearing room no. 303 at the Nikulinskiy District Court of Moscow and hearing room no. 410 at the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow were equipped with metal cages in which nine defendants (seven from 19 December 2013), including the applicant, sat during the hearings.
For a detailed description of the conditions in the hearing rooms used during the trial, see Yaroslav Belousov v. Russia (nos. 2653/13 and 60980/14, §§ 74-77, 4 October 2016).
On 6 June 2013 the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow began a preliminary hearing in a criminal case against ten participants in the demonstration at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.

The ten defendants in the criminal case before the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow were charged with participation in acts of mass disorder and committing acts of violence against police officers.
On 18 June 2013 the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow began the trial on the merits of the criminal case against the ten participants in the demonstration at Bolotnaya Square.
On 5 September 2013 Police Officer T., the alleged victim of the applicant's assault, was examined as a witness at the trial.
Police Officer T. testified that the applicant had impeded him and two other police officers from arresting a protester by grabbing T.'s hand and pushing the officers away.
Police Officer T. testified that the applicant had caused him pain but had not inflicted any injuries.
During the hearing on 5 September 2013 the applicant and his lawyers applied to deprive Police Officer T. of victim status because no harm had been caused to him.
The court refused the applicant's request to deprive Police Officer T. of victim status as unsubstantiated.
On 21 February 2014 the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow found the applicant guilty as charged.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that between 4 p.m. and 8 p.m. on 6 May 2012 at Bolotnaya Square, unidentified persons called those present to move outside the agreed meeting venue and to defy the lawful orders of the police.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that unidentified persons called those present at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012 to use violence, which led to mass disorder accompanied by the use of violence against public officials in connection with the performance of their duties and the destruction of property.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that on 6 May 2012 at 5 p.m. at the latest the defendants acquired the criminal intent to participate in mass disorder and to use violence against police officers.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that participants of the acts of mass disorder threw chunks of tarmac, stones, sticks and other objects at the police, which hit them on various parts of their body.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that the defendants, who participated in the acts of mass disorder, implemented their criminal intent to use violence against public officials by applying physical force which was not a danger to the life or health of those officials.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that the applicant, who was wearing a surgical mask to hide his face, together with unidentified persons, tried to liberate those arrested by the police for a breach of public order and pushed the police officers away.
The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that the applicant used violence against Police Officer T. which did not endanger his life or health.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that from 5 p.m. to 9.40 p.m. on 6 May 2012, when unidentified participants of acts of mass disorder tried to break the police cordon, the applicant acting intentionally grabbed Police Officer T.'s hand and pulled it off the person whom T. was arresting, thus impeding his apprehension, which caused T. pain.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that the applicant, together with unidentified persons, built a line of metal barriers blocking the police's movements and tried to repel the line of police officers with the help of those barriers.
The applicant pleaded not guilty at trial and testified that he had decided to attend the public gathering on 6 May 2012.
The applicant testified that for the purposes of personal security he wore a surgical mask at the demonstration on 6 May 2012.
The applicant testified that he was at the bridge when a blockage occurred and did not see what was happening, but at one point he had been able to proceed with the flow of people towards the stage.

The applicant testified that at the stage area he saw the mass beating of people by police officers and participants of the rally starting to bring forward metal barriers and to put them close to the police officers, trying to protect themselves from the latter.
The applicant testified that he was standing close to the barriers, taking his hands off when the police officers used their truncheons to hit over the barriers.
The applicant testified that he saw a group of five or six police officers who were trying to seize a young man in a green T-shirt and were hitting the man with their truncheons.

The applicant testified that, considering the young man in the green T-shirt was in danger because the police actions were unlawful, he tried to snatch him from the officers' hands by grasping the young man's waistband, pulling it and turning his back to protect him from the truncheon blows.

The applicant testified that he finds it conceivable that in the turmoil he might unintentionally have pushed someone and asked for attention to be paid to Police Officer T.'s statements that T. did not feel any pain.
The applicant testified that after the events at Bolotnaya Square he was arrested and taken to a police vehicle.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow considered the defendants' arguments that they were protecting somebody from police officers or happened to be victims of the police's use of force as farfetched and aimed at the mitigation of their responsibility.
The applicant was sentenced to three years and six months' imprisonment.

The applicant's sentence of three years and six months' imprisonment was calculated on the basis of a three-year prison term under Article 212 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation, partly concurrent with a term of one year and three months under Article 318 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.
The applicant's pre-trial detention counted towards his prison sentence.
The applicant appealed against the judgment of 21 February 2014 of the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow.

In his appeal the applicant complained that the same acts imputed to him had been classified under both Article 212 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation and Article 318 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.
In his appeal the applicant insisted that he had not used violence against Police Officer T. because T. had not suffered any pain or injuries.
On 20 June 2014 the Moscow City Court upheld the first-instance judgment of 21 February 2014 of the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow.

Article 212 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the organisation of mass disorder, accompanied by violence, riot, arson, destruction of property, the use of firearms, explosives and explosive devices, as well as armed resistance to a public official, shall be punishable by four to ten years' deprivation of liberty.

Article 212 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that participation in the types of mass disorder provided for by Article 212 § 1 shall be punishable by three to eight years' deprivation of liberty.

Article 212 § 3 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the instigation of the acts of mass disorder provided for by Article 212 § 1, or the instigation of participation in such acts, or the instigation of violence against citizens, shall be punishable by a restriction of liberty for up to two years, or community service for up to two years, or deprivation of liberty for the same term.

Article 318 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the use of violence which does not endanger life or health, or the threat to use such violence against a public official or his relatives in connection with the performance of his or her duties, shall be punishable by a fine of up to 200,000 roubles or an equivalent of the convicted person's wages for 18 months, or community service for up to five years, or up to five years' deprivation of liberty.

A summary of the relevant domestic law provisions governing pre-trial detention and the practice of the domestic courts in such matters is set out in Zherebin v. Russia (no. 51445/09, §§ 16-25, 24 March 2016).

The applicant's sentence of three years and six months' imprisonment was calculated on the basis of a three-year prison term under Article 212 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation, partly concurrent with a term of one year and three months under Article 318 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.

The applicant appealed against the judgment of 21 February 2014 of the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow.

In his appeal the applicant complained that the same acts imputed to him had been classified under both Article 212 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation and Article 318 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.
In his appeal the applicant insisted that he had not used violence against Police Officer T. because T. had not suffered any pain or injuries.
On 20 June 2014 the Moscow City Court upheld the first-instance judgment of 21 February 2014 of the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow.

Article 212 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the organisation of mass disorder, accompanied by violence, riot, arson, destruction of property, the use of firearms, explosives and explosive devices, as well as armed resistance to a public official, shall be punishable by four to ten years' deprivation of liberty.

Article 212 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that participation in the types of mass disorder provided for by Article 212 § 1 shall be punishable by three to eight years' deprivation of liberty.

Article 212 § 3 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the instigation of the acts of mass disorder provided for by Article 212 § 1, or the instigation of participation in such acts, or the instigation of violence against citizens, shall be punishable by a restriction of liberty for up to two years, or community service for up to two years, or deprivation of liberty for the same term.

Article 318 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the use of violence which does not endanger life or health, or the threat to use such violence against a public official or his relatives in connection with the performance of his or her duties, shall be punishable by a fine of up to 200,000 roubles or an equivalent of the convicted person's wages for 18 months, or community service for up to five years, or up to five years' deprivation of liberty.

A summary of the relevant domestic law provisions governing pre-trial detention and the practice of the domestic courts in such matters is set out in Zherebin v. Russia (no. 51445/09, §§ 16-25, 24 March 2016).

On 6 May 2012 the Moscow city department of the Investigative Committee of the Russian Federation opened criminal proceedings to investigate suspected acts of mass disorder under Article 212 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.

On 6 May 2012 the Moscow city department of the Investigative Committee of the Russian Federation opened criminal proceedings to investigate suspected violence against the police under Article 318 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.
On 18 May 2012 the criminal file opened on 6 May 2012 was transferred to the headquarters of the Investigative Committee of the Russian Federation for further investigation.
On 28 May 2012 an investigation was launched into the criminal offence of organising acts of mass disorder under Article 212 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.
On 28 May 2012 the two criminal cases (mass disorder and organising mass disorder) were joined into a single case.
At the time of his arrest the applicant was a second-year student at the Moscow University of Social Studies.
At the time of his arrest the applicant worked part-time as a courier for an insurance company.
The Basmannyy District Court's detention order of 27 July 2012 referred to the gravity of the charges against the applicant.

The Basmannyy District Court's detention order of 27 July 2012 referred to information about the applicant's character, including a report by Moscow Police's chief of department at the Centre for Counter-Extremism.
According to the report by Moscow Police's chief of department at the Centre for Counter-Extremism, the applicant was an active member of organisations of a destructive character.

According to the report by Moscow Police's chief of department at the Centre for Counter-Extremism, if the applicant were to stay at liberty, he planned to threaten witnesses, abscond and obstruct the investigation.
The Basmannyy District Court concluded on 27 July 2012 that the circumstances gave sufficient grounds to believe that the applicant was likely to flee to avoid the investigation and trial.

The Basmannyy District Court concluded on 27 July 2012 that the circumstances gave sufficient grounds to believe that the applicant was likely to destroy evidence or otherwise obstruct the investigation of the criminal case, which was still at an initial stage.
On 1 August 2012 charges were brought against the applicant under Article 212 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation (participation in acts of mass disorder accompanied by violence).
The applicant was accused of resisting police officers by pushing them away when they were arresting other protestors.
The applicant was accused of trying to liberate protestors who were being arrested by police officers.
On 27 August 2012 the Moscow City Court upheld the detention order of 27 July 2012 issued by the Basmannyy District Court.
On 24 September 2012 the Basmannyy District Court examined an application from the investigator for an extension of the applicant's pre-trial detention.
At the hearing on 24 September 2012 the applicant asked for the preventive measure to be changed to house arrest.
At the hearing on 24 September 2012 the applicant asked for the preventive measure to be changed to a written undertaking not to leave a specified place.
At the hearing on 24 September 2012 the applicant asked for the preventive measure to be changed to bail.
At the hearing on 24 September 2012 the applicant asked for the preventive measure to be changed to personal guarantees.
On 24 September 2012 the Basmannyy District Court granted the investigator's application and extended the applicant's pre-trial detention until 6 November 2012.
The Basmannyy District Court's extension order of 24 September 2012 was based on the finding that the circumstances justifying the original detention order had not changed.
On 1 October 2012 Police Officer T. identified the applicant during an identification parade as a participant in mass disorder who had used violence against him.
Police Officer T. stated that when he and other officers had been arresting a protester, the applicant had grabbed T.'s hand and pulled it off the protestor, thereby causing Police Officer T. pain.
Police Officer L. identified the applicant during an identification parade as a participant in acts of mass disorder who had tried to prevent the police from arresting another protestor.
On 22 October 2012 the Moscow City Court dismissed the applicant's appeal against the extension order of 24 September 2012 issued by the Basmannyy District Court.
On 29 October 2012 the Basmannyy District Court granted an extension of the applicant's pre-trial detention until 6 March 2013, essentially on the same grounds as earlier.
The Basmannyy District Court's extension order of 29 October 2012 noted that the circumstances justifying the detention order had not changed.
In the extension order of 29 October 2012 the Basmannyy District Court dismissed an objection from the applicant to the use of the operational-search reports concerning his character.
In the extension order of 29 October 2012 the Basmannyy District Court rejected the applicant's contesting of the alleged membership of any organisations of a destructive nature.
On 15 November 2012 the charges against the applicant were reformulated.
On 21 December 2012 the charges against the applicant were reformulated.
The reformulated charges stated that the applicant had been wearing a surgical mask to conceal his face during the events of 6 May 2012.
The reformulated charges stated that the applicant had used violence against the police while trying to liberate protestors who had been arrested.
The reformulated charges stated that the applicant had pushed police officers away.
The reformulated charges stated that the applicant had grabbed Police Officer T.'s hand and pulled it off a protester, thereby preventing his arrest.
The reformulated charges stated that the applicant had built a line of metal barriers to block the police and had tried to repel the police with them.
The applicant's alleged offences were additionally classified under Article 318 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation (use of violence against a public official).
On 5 March 2013 the Basmannyy District Court granted a new extension of the applicant's pre-trial detention until 6 July 2013, essentially on the same grounds as before.
On 17 April 2013 the Moscow City Court upheld the extension order of 5 March 2013 issued by the Basmannyy District Court.
On 24 May 2013 the applicant's criminal case was transferred to the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow for the determination of criminal charges.
On 6 June 2013 the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow granted another extension of the applicant's pre-trial detention until 24 November 2013.
The extension order of 6 June 2013 by the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow concerned eleven defendants.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court's extension order of 6 June 2013 was based on the gravity of the charges and the finding that 'the reasons which initially warranted the detention have not changed'.
The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court's extension order of 6 June 2013 was based on the finding that 'no other measures of restraint would secure the aims and goals of the judicial proceedings'.

The applicant's request for an alternative preventive measure was dismissed by the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court on 6 June 2013 on the grounds that no other measure could secure the proper course of justice in the case.
On 2 July 2013 the Moscow City Court upheld the extension order of 6 June 2013 issued by the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow.
On 19 November 2013 the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow granted another extension of pre-trial detention in respect of nine defendants, including the applicant, until 24 February 2014.
The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court's extension order of 19 November 2013 was based on the gravity of the charges and the nature of the offences imputable to the defendants.
On 17 December 2013 the Moscow City Court upheld the extension order of 19 November 2013 issued by the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow.
The applicant was held in remand prison IZ-77/2 for the whole period of his pre-trial detention from 4 September 2012.
According to the applicant, the conditions of his detention in remand prison IZ-77/2 had been poor.

The applicant referred to Lind v. Russia (no. 25664/05, §§ 42 and 58-63, 6 December 2007), in which the Court had previously found a breach of Article 3 of the Convention because of overcrowding in remand prison IZ-77/2 in 2004-2005.

The applicant referred to Zentsov and Others v. Russia (no. 35297/05, §§ 25-29 and 40-44, 23 October 2012), in which the Court had previously found a breach of Article 3 of the Convention because of overcrowding in remand prison IZ-77/2 in 2004-2005.

The applicant referred to Vyatkin v. Russia (no. 18813/06, §§ 26-27 and 38-43, 11 April 2013), in which the Court had previously found a breach of Article 3 of the Convention because of overcrowding in remand prison IZ-77/2 in 2004-2005.

The applicant submitted that his conditions of detention in remand prison IZ-77/2 had been similar to those found to breach Article 3 of the Convention in the cases of Lind v. Russia, Zentsov and Others v. Russia, and Vyatkin v. Russia.

The applicant's description of the conditions of detention during transfer from the remand prison to court and back was identical to those described in Yaroslav Belousov v. Russia (nos. 2653/13 and 60980/14, §§ 69-73, 4 October 2016).

The Government's submissions regarding the conditions of detention during transfer from the remand prison to court and back were identical to those in Yaroslav Belousov v. Russia (nos. 2653/13 and 60980/14, §§ 69-73, 4 October 2016).
The applicant submitted that the convoy room of the Moscow City Court was poorly lit.
The applicant submitted that access to the toilet in the convoy room of the Moscow City Court was limited to once an hour.
The applicant submitted that he had been required to strip naked and to perform sit-ups during the body search conducted in the convoy room of the Moscow City Court.
On 6 June 2013 court proceedings began in hearing room no. 338 at the Moscow City Court.
At the end of July 2013 the court proceedings moved from hearing room no. 338 to hearing room no. 635 at the Moscow City Court.
The defendants, including the applicant, were held in glass cabins in hearing room no. 338 and hearing room no. 635 at the Moscow City Court.
From mid-September 2013 to the end of 2013 the hearings continued at the Nikulinskiy District Court of Moscow in hearing room no. 303.
In January and February 2014 the hearings took place at the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow in hearing room no. 410.

Hearing room no. 303 at the Nikulinskiy District Court of Moscow and hearing room no. 410 at the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow were equipped with metal cages in which nine defendants (seven from 19 December 2013), including the applicant, sat during the hearings.
For a detailed description of the conditions in the hearing rooms used during the trial, see Yaroslav Belousov v. Russia (nos. 2653/13 and 60980/14, §§ 74-77, 4 October 2016).
On 6 June 2013 the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow began a preliminary hearing in a criminal case against ten participants in the demonstration at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.

The ten defendants in the criminal case before the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow were charged with participation in acts of mass disorder and committing acts of violence against police officers.
On 18 June 2013 the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow began the trial on the merits of the criminal case against the ten participants in the demonstration at Bolotnaya Square.
On 5 September 2013 Police Officer T., the alleged victim of the applicant's assault, was examined as a witness at the trial.
Police Officer T. testified that the applicant had impeded him and two other police officers from arresting a protester by grabbing T.'s hand and pushing the officers away.
Police Officer T. testified that the applicant had caused him pain but had not inflicted any injuries.
During the hearing on 5 September 2013 the applicant and his lawyers applied to deprive Police Officer T. of victim status because no harm had been caused to him.
The court refused the applicant's request to deprive Police Officer T. of victim status as unsubstantiated.
On 21 February 2014 the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow found the applicant guilty as charged.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that between 4 p.m. and 8 p.m. on 6 May 2012 at Bolotnaya Square, unidentified persons called those present to move outside the agreed meeting venue and to defy the lawful orders of the police.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that unidentified persons called those present at Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012 to use violence, which led to mass disorder accompanied by the use of violence against public officials in connection with the performance of their duties and the destruction of property.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that on 6 May 2012 at 5 p.m. at the latest the defendants acquired the criminal intent to participate in mass disorder and to use violence against police officers.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that participants of the acts of mass disorder threw chunks of tarmac, stones, sticks and other objects at the police, which hit them on various parts of their body.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that the defendants, who participated in the acts of mass disorder, implemented their criminal intent to use violence against public officials by applying physical force which was not a danger to the life or health of those officials.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that the applicant, who was wearing a surgical mask to hide his face, together with unidentified persons, tried to liberate those arrested by the police for a breach of public order and pushed the police officers away.
The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that the applicant used violence against Police Officer T. which did not endanger his life or health.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that from 5 p.m. to 9.40 p.m. on 6 May 2012, when unidentified participants of acts of mass disorder tried to break the police cordon, the applicant acting intentionally grabbed Police Officer T.'s hand and pulled it off the person whom T. was arresting, thus impeding his apprehension, which caused T. pain.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow held that the applicant, together with unidentified persons, built a line of metal barriers blocking the police's movements and tried to repel the line of police officers with the help of those barriers.
The applicant pleaded not guilty at trial and testified that he had decided to attend the public gathering on 6 May 2012.
The applicant testified that for the purposes of personal security he wore a surgical mask at the demonstration on 6 May 2012.
The applicant testified that he was at the bridge when a blockage occurred and did not see what was happening, but at one point he had been able to proceed with the flow of people towards the stage.

The applicant testified that at the stage area he saw the mass beating of people by police officers and participants of the rally starting to bring forward metal barriers and to put them close to the police officers, trying to protect themselves from the latter.
The applicant testified that he was standing close to the barriers, taking his hands off when the police officers used their truncheons to hit over the barriers.
The applicant testified that he saw a group of five or six police officers who were trying to seize a young man in a green T-shirt and were hitting the man with their truncheons.

The applicant testified that, considering the young man in the green T-shirt was in danger because the police actions were unlawful, he tried to snatch him from the officers' hands by grasping the young man's waistband, pulling it and turning his back to protect him from the truncheon blows.

The applicant testified that he finds it conceivable that in the turmoil he might unintentionally have pushed someone and asked for attention to be paid to Police Officer T.'s statements that T. did not feel any pain.
The applicant testified that after the events at Bolotnaya Square he was arrested and taken to a police vehicle.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow considered the defendants' arguments that they were protecting somebody from police officers or happened to be victims of the police's use of force as farfetched and aimed at the mitigation of their responsibility.
The applicant was sentenced to three years and six months' imprisonment.

The applicant's sentence of three years and six months' imprisonment was calculated on the basis of a three-year prison term under Article 212 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation, partly concurrent with a term of one year and three months under Article 318 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.
The applicant's pre-trial detention counted towards his prison sentence.
